title: Tweet Counts Per Frequency
statement:
Build a class `TweetCounts` that logs tweets by name and time (in seconds) and reports how many fall into each slice of a time window.

- `TweetCounts()` starts with no tweets logged.
- `recordTweet(tweetName, time)` logs one tweet called `tweetName` at second `time`. The same name may be logged many times, even at the same second, and every entry counts.
- `getTweetCountsPerFrequency(freq, tweetName, startTime, endTime)` looks at the inclusive window `[startTime, endTime]`. `freq` is `"minute"`, `"hour"` or `"day"`, meaning slices of 60, 3600 or 86400 seconds. Cut the window into consecutive slices of that length starting at `startTime`: `[startTime, startTime + len - 1]`, then the next `len` seconds, and so on; the final slice stops at `endTime` and may be shorter. Return a list with, for each slice in order, the number of logged `tweetName` tweets whose time lies inside it (zero counts included).
constraints: At most 10^4 calls are made to recordTweet and getTweetCountsPerFrequency in total

signature.name: TweetCounts
methods: List<Integer> getTweetCountsPerFrequency(String freq, String tweetName, int startTime, int endTime)

notes:
## Intuition

Each query only cares about one tweet name and a window of at most 10,001 seconds, and the number of slices is just `(endTime - startTime) / len + 1`. A hash map from name to that name's times isolates the right tweets; keeping each list sorted lets a query jump straight to the first time inside the window and stop as soon as it passes `endTime`. Every time found lands in slice `(time - startTime) / len`, rounded down. A brute force that rescans all tweets for every slice also works, just more slowly.

## Approach

1. Keep `times`, a map from each tweet name to a sorted list of its times.
2. `firstAtLeast(list, time)` binary-searches for the first index whose value is at least `time`.
3. `recordTweet` creates the list if needed and inserts `time` at that index, so the list stays sorted.
4. `getTweetCountsPerFrequency` turns `freq` into a slice length `size` and makes `counts` with one zero per slice.
5. Starting at `firstAtLeast(list, startTime)`, walk while the time is at most `endTime`, adding one to slice `floor((time - startTime) / size)`.
6. Return `counts`.

## Example 1, step by step

- After the first three records, `times` holds `"tweet3" → [0, 10, 60]`.
- `("minute", "tweet3", 0, 59)`: one slice. The walk starts at index 0, counts 0 and 10 into slice 0, and stops at 60 > 59: `[2]`.
- `("minute", "tweet3", 0, 60)`: two slices. 0 and 10 go to slice 0, 60 goes to slice `(60 - 0) / 60 = 1`: `[2, 1]`.
- `recordTweet("tweet3", 120)` makes the list `[0, 10, 60, 120]`.
- `("hour", "tweet3", 0, 210)`: one slice of 3600 seconds holds all four: `[4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: `recordTweet` is O(n) for the array insert (O(log n) to find the spot); a query is O(log n + k + w / size), with k tweets inside the window and w its width.
- Space: O(n) for all stored times.

## Pitfalls

- Windows and slices are inclusive at both ends: a tweet at exactly `endTime` counts.
- Slices start at `startTime`, not at a multiple of 60; compute the slot from `time - startTime`.
- Empty slices must still appear as `0`, and an unknown name returns all zeros.
- Repeated tweets at the same second all count; do not deduplicate.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `times` | map from tweet name to its sorted list of times |
| `list` | the sorted times for one name |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary search bounds and midpoint |
| `size` | slice length in seconds for `freq` |
| `counts` | the answer, one count per slice |
| `index` | position of the current time while walking the window |

narration.3: One map holds, for every tweet name, its times in sorted order.
narration.9: Binary search: shrink the range until left is the first index whose time is at least the target.
narration.11: A time smaller than the target means the answer lies to the right of mid.
narration.17: left is now where the target time belongs in the sorted list.
narration.21: The first tweet with this name gets an empty list.
narration.25: Insert the time at its sorted position so later queries can binary-search.
narration.29: Turn the frequency name into a slice length in seconds.
narration.30: One counter per slice, all starting at zero; the last slice may be short.
narration.31: An unknown name behaves like an empty list.
narration.32: Jump to the first stored time that is not before the window starts.
narration.33: Walk forward while the time is still inside the window.
narration.34: The offset from startTime, divided by the slice length, picks the slice to count.
narration.37: Return the per-slice counts in order.
